rv.q: And Platt is superb, bringing his vocal range and agility to Sonnenblick’s nostalgic songs.
Midnight at the Never Get sees music as both heartbreak and cure.

The way in which Sonnenblick, partly through Trevor’s casual asides, creates in Arthur a fictional superstar of the great American songbook, is a delicious blurring of reality and theatrical invention.
Platt’s sheer star power makes it a night to remember.
Taken as a song cycle describing the arc of a relationship against an evocative urban backdrop, it’s great fun.

Sonnenblick’s songs – impressively drawing on the traditions of the Great American Songbook – have a maturity that’s a world away from his fizzy earworms for Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters and prove his range as a composer.
But structurally, it's frustratingly old school – imprisoned by a wistful nostalgia that won't allow Platt's real talents to break free.
It’s a lost world evoked in immaculate detail in David Cromer’s production: a bold, unconventional drama that doesn’t, in the end, pay quite as much attention to the inner lives of the two lovers.
It’s a rare piece of musical theatre that trusts its audience as completely as this, and is all the more moving because of it.
Midnight at The Never Get proves to be a beautifully crafted piece of musical storytelling which is warm, witty and quietly powerful.
Platt’s vibrato-tinged voice is perfectly suited to the material and it’s a joy to witness his talents from such close quarters.
This is a rare opportunity to see a singular talent at the top of his game giving full virtuoso flex to material that feels ripe with embryonic potential.

Bedecked in a bronze coloured suit which serves as a carapace, he delivers torch-songs, comedy numbers and ballads, each of which could feasibly be drawn from the Great American Songbook such is the quality of their evident musical influences and panache.
Midnight at the Never Get doesn’t do enough with the device to land the empathy it is looking for.
This production is as special as theatre gets, furthered by Ben Platt's phenomenal performance.
I truly, wholeheartedly believe that I have seen something that can and should fundamentally shape the next stage of West End theatre.
The story builds, the songs throb emotion, crystallize deep feeling; Trevor never changes.
Midnight at the Never Get is tender, thoughtful, and tenacious.
Sonnenblick's richly crafted score and Platt's striking performance make Midnight at the Never Get a production well worth seeking out.

cn.t: Ben Platt dazzles in this intimate 1960s gay love story, with critics praising his vocals and the metatheatrical cabaret staging, though some find the 90-minute musical schmaltzy and dramatically thin.
